Underscore-prefixed fields (_contract, _provenance, _internal, _guard) NEVER reach the DOM. null/missing = render nothing. Footnotes render ONCE in a single 'Notes & assumptions' section above the contact form; a footnote's source_url may render as a small domain chip, never as a naked URL in body copy. copy.framing: Two ways to partner — a genuine choice. Boston's landscape leans Enable, with proven public operators alongside.
copy.enable_track: Grant landing access at existing public piers and a permitting pathway for a pilot corridor. Private capital finances the fleet; privately committed employer demand fills the seats. The ask is access, not money.
copy.operate_track: Massachusetts public bodies already own and operate ferry fleets. Navier vessels can be procured the way transit vehicles are procured — to build, run, or augment the public water network.

operate_proof_points.proof: Owns vessels, funds routes, and directly procures operating contracts across nine ferry routes — the clearest public vessel-operator precedent in this market.
Funds and manages the Seaport Ferry (Lovejoy Wharf–Fan Pier–East Boston), launched on a pilot basis.

copy.headline: Your speed rules were written for boats that make wake.
copy.framing: Harbor speed rules exist to control wake, wash, noise, and disturbance — outcomes a foiling, electric Navier satisfies inherently.
copy.ask: Our ask: measure us. Where independent wake and noise measurement shows the rule's purpose is served, grant route-specific relief through the mechanism your own regulations already provide.

_provenance.body_v1: Harbor speed rules exist to control wake, wash, noise, and disturbance. Massachusetts law already draws the right distinction: 323 CMR 2 separately prohibits harmful wash — an outcome a foiling Navier satisfies inherently — while capping headway speed at 6 mph in regulated situations. The regulations even contain an existing relief mechanism: marked-channel permission granted by an authorized marine-enforcement agency.
_provenance.precedent_v1: Precedent exists: on Region Stockholm's Route 89, a Candela P-12 electric hydrofoil operated at ~22 knots in a ~12-knot zone under a low-wake speed exemption (attributed to Länsstyrelsen, the county administrative board).

rule_basis.detail: headway speed defined as minimum steerage speed, not over 6 mph

prohibits wash thrown into other vessels/floats; requires headway speed near marinas/floats/swimmers and in channels unless an authorized marine-enforcement agency permits otherwise with marked speeds

_provenance.base_times_policy_v1: All map and trip times on this page respect posted limits. No exemption is assumed. Relief renders only in the labeled 'what relief unlocks' layer, which for Boston carries no numbers this pass. Now carried by fn5.

expander.title: What speed-rule relief unlocks
body: Harbor speed rules exist to control wake, wash, noise, and disturbance. Massachusetts law already draws that distinction: it separately prohibits harmful wash — an outcome a foiling vessel satisfies inherently — and it already contains a relief mechanism granted by marine-enforcement agencies.
Our ask: measure us. Where independent wake and noise measurement shows the rule's purpose is served, grant route-specific relief through the mechanism your regulations already provide.
Precedent: Stockholm's public transport authority runs an electric hydrofoil ferry at roughly twice the posted zone speed under a low-wake exemption.

navier_intro.title: Meet the vessel

copy.headline: Zero-emission. Near-silent. Almost no wake.
copy.subline: Navier is a U.S. builder of electric hydrofoil vessels — the traits that matter for harbor rules and harbor neighbors are built into the hull, not bolted on.
copy.body: The N45 Explorer carries 30 passengers at a foilborne cruise speed of about 30 knots, lifted clear of the water for a smooth, wake-free ride. The smaller N30 Quanta carries 8. Foiling cuts energy use by up to ~90% versus a conventional planing hull, and both vessels run near-silent on electric power.

tech_chips.value: up to ~90% less than a planing hull

reference.title: Reference

copy.intro: Boston Harbor's water-transportation landscape spans state, regional, and municipal bodies. We seek conversations — nothing here implies approval, endorsement, or commitment by any body named.

bodies.role: Runs nine public ferry routes; owns vessels and procures operating contracts — the region's proven public water-transit operator.
State transportation secretariat; leads the cross-agency Water Transportation Study (Summer 2025–Summer 2026) scoping five stations on this network.
Funds and manages the Seaport Ferry serving Fan Pier and Lovejoy Wharf.
Waterfront planning and Municipal Harbor Plans for the South Boston, Downtown, and East Boston waterfronts.
Port authority and underlying landowner at Commonwealth Pier; grants landing access at existing public docks.
Public-trust licensing for tideland structures; existing landings used as-is generally need no new license — modifications do.
Landowner at Squantum Point Park (Quincy) and the Hingham ferry terminal, which the MBTA operates under long-term lease.
State-chartered body coordinating port development within Salem Harbor, including Salem Wharf.

bodies.body: Harbor towns and cities — Hull, Winthrop, Quincy, Hingham
bodies.role: Own or co-manage their municipal landings (Pemberton Point, Winthrop Town Landing, Squantum Point partnership, Hewitts Cove harbor operations).
Steward of part of Charlestown Navy Yard; carries a federal mandate to improve Boston Harbor Islands access through public water transportation.
